analysis.one_liner: Banned nearly all tobacco advertising, sponsorship, and branded packaging to keep cigarettes away from children.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote, despite 42 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stripped tobacco marketing down to plain black-on-white text: no cartoon characters or human figures, no billboards within 500 feet of schools, no stadium or race car ads, no free samples or coupons, no sponsorship of sports or music events, and no paid appearances in movies, TV shows, or on toys. Cigarette packs themselves would have carried no logos, colors, or pictures. Violations could be stopped by lawsuits in federal court, and products marketed illegally would be treated as misbranded drugs under food and drug law.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, who the bill's findings say make up the vast majority of new smokers and are the group most influenced by image-heavy ads and sports sponsorship. Smokers and former smokers also benefit from less marketing that normalizes smoking, and the public at large saves some of the estimated $22 billion a year spent treating smoking-related disease, about $4.2 billion of which was paid by the federal government.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children and teens targeted by tobacco marketing

how_it_helps.text: Would have required plain packages and ads: no human figures, brand logos, symbols, or pictures, with black print on a white background only — removing the imagery the bill says has the greatest impact on people under 18.
Would have banned tobacco ads from sports stadiums and equipment and from anywhere within 500 feet of a school attended by students under 18.

Would have ended free samples and coupons for free or discounted tobacco, sponsorship of athletic, music, and artistic events, brand-named nontobacco merchandise, and paid product placement in movies, TV, plays, and on toys.
The bill's findings state that over half of high-school seniors who smoke began by eighth grade, and that tobacco advertising is regularly seen by people under 18 — the group the restrictions target.

Gave federal district courts power to hear lawsuits to restrain violations, and treated products advertised or packaged in violation as misbranded drugs under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, giving regulators a second enforcement path.
Explicitly preserved the FTC's existing authority and let state and local governments adopt equal or stricter rules, so the federal floor would not roll back tougher local laws.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, which the bill says spent close to $2.5 billion a year on marketing, would have lost nearly every promotional tool they had. Advertising agencies, billboard owners, magazines, and other media would lose tobacco ad revenue, and sports leagues, race teams, concert promoters, and other events would lose tobacco sponsorship money, with only a three-year phase-out for contracts signed before enactment. Tobacco retailers would lose point-of-sale displays and sampling, and tobacco-state economies would bear reduced sales.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tobacco companies and their marketing partners

drawbacks.text: The restriction is extremely broad: it bans brand imagery even in advertising seen almost entirely by adults, going far beyond the child-targeting measures like the school-zone billboard ban and the toy-placement ban.

It would have wiped out an estimated $2.5 billion a year in tobacco marketing spending, costing advertising agencies, billboard companies, magazines, and tobacco-state jobs real income, not just the tobacco companies themselves.
Sports teams, race circuits, and arts events that relied on tobacco sponsorship would lose that money, with only a three-year grandfather period for contracts already signed when the law took effect.

Commercial speech of this sweep faced serious First Amendment questions even in 1989, since courts were already scrutinizing bans on truthful advertising of lawful products; a court fight was a foreseeable cost of the design.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but narrow and mostly borne by one industry and its vendors, while the benefit — fewer children recruited into a product the bill calls the only one that kills when used as intended — is large and durable. The phase-ins (one year generally, two for billboards, three for existing sponsorship contracts) and the carve-outs for pre-1986 corporate names show the drafters tried to soften the blow to sponsors and legacy brands. This was an aggressive bill, but not a reckless one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, sent to the health subcommittee two weeks later, and never received a markup, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Synar introduced the bill on March 20, 1989, joined by 18 original cosponsors from both parties, including senior members such as John Dingell's committee colleagues Ed Markey, Henry Waxman, and John Conyers.
The bill went to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction and to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment on April 3, 1989.
The cosponsor list grew to 42 members — 34 Democrats and 8 Republicans — but no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened.
The bill sat without action for the rest of the 101st Congress and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers kept their roughly $2.5 billion annual marketing operation intact, along with the advertising agencies, billboard owners, media outlets, and sports and entertainment events that depend on tobacco money.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco companies and their marketing partners

for.name: Mike Synar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan set of original cosponsors including members of both parties.

for.name: 8 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support in both parties.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair John Dingell and the committee's Health and the Environment Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittee two weeks after introduction and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill sat untouched for the rest of the two-year Congress.

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.what_they_did: Fought advertising and marketing restriction legislation through lobbying and by cultivating allies from tobacco-growing states.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded; its 42 cosponsors split 34 Democrats and 8 Republicans, showing cross-party support but only a small share of the Republican caucus.

industries.note: The bill would have eliminated nearly every marketing tool: branded packages, imagery in ads, billboards near schools, event sponsorship, sampling, coupons, and paid placements in entertainment. The industry's growth depends on recruiting new smokers, and the bill's findings state most new smokers are minors, so its interest ran directly against the bill's public health purpose.

industries.industry: Advertising agencies, billboard owners, and print media
industries.note: Tobacco marketing was a large revenue stream; the bill would have cut ads down to text and plain package images and phased out billboards over two years.

industries.industry: Sports, racing, and entertainment event organizers
industries.note: Tobacco sponsorship of athletic, music, and artistic events would have been banned, with a three-year phase-out for contracts already signed.
Point-of-sale displays and free sampling would have been restricted, and sharply reduced marketing would be expected to cut overall sales in tobacco-dependent regions.
